title: Thin slices of expressive behavior as predictors of interpersonal consequences: A meta-analysis.
finding: Meta-analysis (38 results, observations under 5 min): per authors, overall accuracy of predicting objective outcomes from brief expressive behaviour was r = .39; observations under half a minute predicted no worse than 4-5 min ones, and the channel (face, speech, body, tone of voice) did not matter.
why_for_us: Viewers will have a usable judgement of a character within the first seconds, and more screen time will not sharpen it; the opening shot must already carry the expressive behaviour we want judged.

title: First Impressions: Making Up Your Mind After a 100-Ms Exposure to a Face
finding: Five experiments (one per trait): per authors, judgements of attractiveness, likeability, trustworthiness, competence and aggressiveness after 100 ms correlated highly with unconstrained judgements; longer exposure did not raise the correlations, mainly raised confidence, and from 100 to 500 ms judgements became more negative.
why_for_us: The first frame of a face fixes trust and competence impressions before any line is spoken, so the AI-generated face (expression, gaze, framing) has to be chosen for frame one, not for the scene as a whole.

title: Inferences of Competence from Faces Predict Election Outcomes
finding: Per authors, competence inferred from faces alone after a 1-second exposure predicted U.S. congressional election outcomes above chance (68.8% of 2004 Senate races) and related linearly to margin of victory; the effect was specific to competence.
why_for_us: For a professional audience (notaries), the on-screen professional should read as competent in the first second; a competence cue is more consequential than a likeability cue.

title: Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression!
finding: Three studies: per authors, visual-appeal ratings of web homepages shown for 500 ms were highly consistent across repeated phases, and ratings after 50 ms correlated highly with those after 500 ms, so visual appeal is assessed within about 50 ms.
why_for_us: The landing page and the video's first frame/thumbnail are judged on visual appeal before anything is read; composition and colour of frame one decide, not copy.

title: The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites: Working towards understanding aesthetic judgments
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no finding or numbers were extracted in this session; per title and keywords the paper studies visual complexity, prototypicality and presentation time in first-impression aesthetic judgements of websites.
why_for_us: Flag for full-text reading before using it to argue for a simple, familiar-looking first frame and landing page; do not cite numbers from it yet.

title: How Do You Say ‘Hello’? Personality Impressions from Brief Novel Voices
finding: Online rating experiment (N=320 listeners, 64 sub-second utterances of 'hello', 10 traits): per authors, personality judgements of unfamiliar voices were consistent across listeners and summarised by a two-dimensional space of Valence (trust, likeability) and Dominance, each driven by different vocal acoustics.
why_for_us: The first word of the AI voice already sets trust and dominance impressions, so voices should be auditioned on their first sub-second word, and the opening word scripted to carry warmth.

title: Can we undo our first impressions? The role of reinterpretation in reversing implicit evaluations.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Seven experiments: per authors, implicit evaluations of a novel person were fully reversed only when new information prompted reinterpretation of what was learned earlier, required at least moderate cognitive resources, and the revised evaluation was still present 3 days later.
why_for_us: A bad first impression of a character or of the product can be repaired only by a later beat that reframes the opening itself (a twist), not by simply adding positive material afterwards.

title: First Impressions Matter: An Experimental Investigation of Online Financial Advice
finding: Incentivised discrete choice experiment: per authors, consumers more often follow advisers who give good advice before bad, opinions of adviser quality can be manipulated through the order and difficulty of advice topics, and clients also use professional credentials to guide choices (no effect sizes in the abstract).
why_for_us: Closest evidence to our case (trust in a professional adviser): the first claim the product or character makes must be one the notary can immediately verify as correct; put the easy, checkable truth first.

title: Forming impressions of personality.
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no finding or numbers were extracted in this session; the record confirms the classic 1946 impression-formation paper by S. E. Asch (vol. 41, pp. 258-290).
why_for_us: Cite only as the historical origin of primacy in impression formation; the working rule (lead with the trait you want to colour everything else) needs a source whose abstract we have read.

title: The serial position effect of free recall.
finding: Per the abstract, the serial position curve shows a steep primacy effect over the first 3 or 4 words of a list, an S-shaped recency effect over the last 8 words, and a flat asymptote between them (list-learning experiments; designs not given in the part of the abstract available).
why_for_us: In a 60-90 s episode the first few items and the last ones are what is recalled; the product name or the problem should sit in the opening and the closing seconds, not in the middle.

title: Order in Choice: Effects of Serial Position on Preferences
finding: Large-scale tasting experiment with sets of 2-5 wines sampled in sequence: per authors, the first wine had a large advantage in the end-of-sequence choice (primacy), while knowledgeable participants showed a recency effect in longer sequences.
why_for_us: When an episode shows several options or arguments, the one we want chosen goes first for lay viewers; expert viewers (notaries on legal content) may weight the last one, so repeat it at the end.

title: Message Order Effects in Persuasion: An Attitude Strength Perspective
finding: Review plus two factorial experiments (message order x personal relevance): per authors, conditions fostering high message elaboration produce primacy (the first message dominates final judgements), whereas low elaboration produces recency (the second message dominates).
why_for_us: Primacy is not universal: the opening argument wins only if the viewer is processing attentively, so the first seconds must establish personal relevance for notaries; for a distracted scroller the last message counts more.

title: Duration neglect in retrospective evaluations of affective episodes.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Two experiments with film clips (Study 1 N=32, Study 2 N=96): per authors, clip duration had only small effects on retrospective evaluations, which behaved like a weighted average of 'snapshots' of the momentary affective experience.
why_for_us: Overall liking of an episode will depend on a few intense moments rather than on length, so a strong opening does not excuse a flat peak or ending; plan one clear high point as well as the hook.

title: All’s well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no finding or numbers were extracted in this session; per title and keywords it is a meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect in retrospective evaluation.
why_for_us: The right source for the limits of the peak-end rule, but its effect sizes must be read from the full text before we weight openings against endings in the episode template.

title: The Limited Capacity Model of Mediated Message Processing
finding: Theory paper: per the abstract it presents an information-processing model of how mediated messages are processed, applies it to television viewing, gives a measure for each part of the model and reviews supporting evidence (no effect sizes in the abstract).
why_for_us: Gives the frame for the opening: attention-getting structural features cost processing capacity, so the first seconds should not pair an attention grab with dense information.

title: The Effects of Related and Unrelated Cuts on Television Viewers' Attention, Processing Capacity, and Memory
finding: Experiment: per authors, both related and unrelated cuts elicited cardiac orienting responses; reaction times were slower after unrelated cuts (more capacity needed), and memory was better for information after related cuts, especially visual memory.
why_for_us: A cut in the first seconds does pull attention, but if it jumps to unrelated content the next line is remembered worse; keep early cuts within the same scene and put the key line after a related cut.

title: The Effects of Edits on Arousal, Attention, and Memory for Television Messages: When an Edit Is an Edit Can an Edit Be Too Much?
finding: Experiment varying the rate of edits (camera changes within the same visual scene) from slow to very fast: per authors, physiological arousal, self-reported arousal and memory all increased with edit rate, suggesting edits raise attention and encoding without significantly raising cognitive load.
why_for_us: Fast same-scene camera changes are a safe way to lift arousal in the opening; the benefit reported is for edits inside one scene, not for scene changes.

title: Influence of attentional capture on oculomotor control.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology Human Perception & Performance
finding: Eye-movement experiments: per the abstract, while searching for a colour singleton the eye in many instances moved toward a task-irrelevant abrupt onset, and top-down control could not entirely prevent capture by the onset.
why_for_us: Something appearing abruptly in frame pulls the eyes even against the viewer's intent; use one onset at the point we want looked at and avoid competing onsets (captions, logos popping in) elsewhere.

title: Motion Onset Captures Attention
finding: Three experiments: per authors, moving items had no advantage over static ones, but items that had just started to move did, even though the motion was uninformative; detection was independent of the number of distractors when the target had a motion onset.
why_for_us: Continuous motion in the opening shot does not hold attention by itself; what captures is the start of a movement, so begin on a still beat and let the key object or person start moving in the first second.

title: Catching Eyes: Effects of Social and Nonsocial Cues on Attention Capture
finding: Experiment with four faces switching gaze: per authors, the greatest response-time facilitation occurred at the location of a sudden onset of direct gaze; with a 900 ms delay direct gaze still facilitated while the motion cue became inhibitory, indicating independent social and non-social attention channels.
why_for_us: A character turning to look straight into the lens in the first second combines two capture cues, and the gaze effect outlasts the motion effect; open on the turn-to-camera rather than on a face already staring.

title: Effect of Vocal-Pitch Difference on Automatic Attention to Voice Changes in Audio Messages
finding: Within-subjects experiment (N=41, 12 radio commercials, heart rate and recognition memory): per authors, pitch difference between speakers affects the orienting response to a voice change and thereby recognition memory, and voice changes placed early in the message (first 20 s) gave the best attentional result.
why_for_us: Switching between two clearly different AI voices early in the episode is a cheap orienting device; cast voices with a marked pitch difference and place the first voice change in the opening seconds.

title: The Wick in the Candle of Learning: Epistemic Curiosity Activates Reward Circuitry and Enhances Memory
finding: fMRI plus behavioural studies with trivia questions: per authors, curiosity correlated with caudate activity, subjects spent more scarce resources (tokens or waiting time) to get answers when more curious, and higher curiosity predicted better recall of surprising answers 1 to 2 weeks later (sample sizes not in the abstract).
why_for_us: An opening question the viewer wants answered buys waiting time and makes the answer memorable, so pose a question notaries are curious about and let the product be the surprising answer.

title: States of Curiosity Modulate Hippocampus-Dependent Learning via the Dopaminergic Circuit
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no finding or numbers were extracted in this session; per title and keywords it concerns curiosity states, incidental learning and memory enhancement via dopaminergic circuits.
why_for_us: Potentially supports placing the brand inside a curiosity window (incidental material learned while curious), but this must be confirmed from the full text before it becomes a rule.

title: Click bait: Forward-reference as lure in online news headlines
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no finding or numbers were extracted in this session; per title and keywords it analyses forward-reference in online news headlines as a curiosity and anticipation lure.
why_for_us: Source for the definition of the forward-reference device ('this is what happened when...') in titles; it gives no click data in the record, so treat it as description, not proof that the device works.

title: You won't believe what's in this paper! Clickbait, relevance and the curiosity gap
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no finding or numbers were extracted in this session; per title it is a pragmatics (relevance-theoretic) account of clickbait and the curiosity gap.
why_for_us: Conceptual vocabulary for writing episode titles; no behavioural evidence can be taken from this record.

title: Negativity drives online news consumption
finding: Randomised headline trials from Upworthy (N = 22,743 RCTs, ~105,000 headline variations, ~5.7 million clicks, over 370 million impressions): per authors, negative words increased and positive words decreased click-through; for a headline of average length each additional negative word raised CTR by 2.3%. OpenAlex also lists a 2025 OSF reproduction report with an authors' response.
why_for_us: Titles and email subjects framed on the problem or loss (a deed rejected, a deadline missed) should out-click upbeat benefit titles; the effect per word is small and comes from general-news readers, so test it on notaries.

title: Effective Headlines of Newspaper Articles in a Digital Environment
finding: Field data from the Blendle online kiosk (triples of original headline, rewritten headline and newsletter CTR): per authors, most but not all 'clickbait features' gave a statistically significant increase in clicks, yet the effectiveness of a headline could not be predicted from its clickbait features alone.
why_for_us: Stylistic title tricks help on average but do not make a title predictable; A/B test real titles instead of applying a checklist.

title: Does Clickbait Actually Attract More Clicks? Three Clickbait Studies You Must Read
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Three studies (quasi-experiment with classifier-labelled headlines, controlled experiment varying one clickbait characteristic of the same story, computational analysis of sharing data): per authors, clickbait did not generate more curiosity than non-clickbait in Studies 1 and 2, and four detectors agreed on a classification only 47% of the time.
why_for_us: Lists, questions and 'you won't believe' wording are not reliably more curiosity-inducing than plain titles; do not assume a clickbait-style title or first line will bring notaries in.

title: The (Null) Effects of Clickbait Headlines on Polarization, Trust, and Learning
finding: Two randomised experiments (Facebook-recruited sample with high clickbait preference and an MTurk sample): per authors, older people and non-Democrats had a higher preference for clickbait, but reading clickbait headlines did not change affective polarisation, information retention or trust in media.
why_for_us: A teasing title is unlikely by itself to damage trust or retention, so the risk of curiosity-gap titles lies in disappointing content, not in the title style; preference for such titles varies by audience.

title: What makes you click? The effect of question headlines on readership in computer-mediated communication
finding: Two field experiments: per authors, question headlines generated significantly more readership than declarative ones, self-referencing questions ('you') did best and beat rhetorical questions, but the effect varied across message topics (no sizes in the abstract).
why_for_us: Supports a self-referencing question as title or first line ('Is your register ready for...?'), with the caveat that the effect is topic-dependent and contradicted by later Upworthy data (see OU031).

title: Peeking, Pooling, and a Locked Split: A Pre-registered Replication of the Question-Headline Effect on the Upworthy Archive, with an Always-Valid Sequential Testing Module
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
finding: Single-author, non-peer-reviewed Zenodo preprint: per the author, a random-effects meta-analysis of 465 randomised Upworthy headline tests gives a pooled odds ratio of 0.8645 (95% CI 0.8335-0.8966) for question headlines, i.e. fewer clicks, with large heterogeneity (I squared 75.8%); in simulation, peeking seven times at a 5% test rejected 16.32% of null streams.
why_for_us: Counter-evidence to 'open with a question': on a large real archive question titles lost on average; also a warning not to stop our own title A/B tests early.

title: Understanding in-video dropouts and interaction peaks inonline lecture videos
finding: Field data (second-by-second interaction data, 862 videos, four edX MOOCs): per authors, dropout was higher in longer videos, in re-watching sessions and in tutorials; in a sample of 80 videos, 61% of interaction peaks accompanied visual transitions such as a slide-to-classroom switch.
why_for_us: Viewers return to and act on visual transitions, so each new idea in the episode should start on a visible change of shot; shorter runtime lowers in-video dropout.

title: Attention during Lectures: Beyond Ten Minutes
finding: Narrative review of note-taking, observation, self-report and physiological studies: per authors, the research behind the claim that student attention declines 10 to 15 minutes into a lecture gives little support for it, and most studies ignored individual differences.
why_for_us: Fixed attention-span numbers ('you have N seconds/minutes') are not evidence-based; plan for individual variation and re-engagement points rather than a magic cut-off.

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Advance Organizers on Learning and Retention
finding: Meta-analysis (135 published and unpublished studies): per authors, advance organizers had a facilitative effect on both learning and retention (effect size not given in the abstract).
why_for_us: A one-line orientation at the start ('here is what goes wrong with X and how it ends') helps the rest stick; an opening can frame as well as tease.

title: The limited effects of prequestions on learning from authentic lecture videos.
venue: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
finding: Two experiments with authentic lecture videos over 20 min: per authors, the prequestion group outperformed controls overall and on prequestioned information, but non-prequestioned information was not different (Exp. 1) or only marginally better (Exp. 2); the benefit did not interact with interest.
why_for_us: An opening question improves memory mainly for the thing asked about, so the opening question must target exactly the point (the product benefit) we want remembered.

title: ManyClasses 2: The effects of prequestions on media interactions and learning.
finding: Multi-site classroom experiment (30 classes, n = 1,571, two online lecture videos, one preceded by ungraded prequestions): per authors, prequestions improved delayed learning on average, but caused some students to skip the video entirely and did not increase the amount viewed; benefits were moderated by answering the prequestions correctly.
why_for_us: Opening with a question does not make people watch longer and can make some leave; use the question to prime the right mental model, and keep it easy enough for a notary to answer.

title: Keep it Coherent: A Meta-Analysis of the Seductive Details Effect
finding: The OpenAlex search record showed no abstract, so no numbers were extracted in this session; per title it is a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect (interesting but irrelevant additions to instructional material).
why_for_us: Relevant to the temptation to open with an eye-catching but off-topic gag; effect sizes must be read from the full text before we rule on irrelevant hooks.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: How Figurative Language and Gesturing in Entrepreneurial Pitches Influences Investment Judgments
finding: Qualitative field study followed by an experiment on investors' propensity to invest: per authors, variation in the type of language (literal vs figurative) had limited effects, while using gestures to depict and symbolise the business idea had strong positive effects.
why_for_us: In a pitch-like opening, show the idea with the hands or with on-screen action rather than polishing the metaphor in the first line; depiction beats wording.

title: Persuading Investors: A Video-Based Study
finding: NBER working paper using machine-learning coding of full start-up pitch videos plus an experiment: per authors, more positive (passionate, warm) delivery increases funding probability, yet conditional on funding high-positivity start-ups underperform, and delivery works mainly by leading investors to inaccurate beliefs.
why_for_us: Warm, energetic delivery from the first second persuades regardless of substance; useful for the AI voice and face, with the ethical caveat that delivery must not oversell what the SaaS does.

title: A Cognitive Model of the Antecedents and Consequences of Satisfaction Decisions
finding: Two-stage field study (flu inoculation programme): per the abstract, satisfaction is modelled as a function of expectation and expectancy disconfirmation, and satisfaction in turn influences attitude change and purchase intention; results support the scheme.
why_for_us: Whatever the opening promises becomes the expectation the product is judged against; the hook should promise only what the first session of the SaaS visibly delivers.

title: Design and Evaluation of Optimal Free Trials
finding: Large-scale SaaS field experiment on trial length: per authors, shorter trials on average maximised acquisition, retention and profitability; long stretches of inactivity at the end of a trial were associated with lower conversion; a personalised policy improved subscriptions by 6.8% over a uniform 30-day trial, with beginners more responsive to short trials.
why_for_us: For the SaaS the episodes promote, early activity matters more than a long window; the call to action should lead to an immediate first use, not to 'try it sometime in 30 days'.

title: The Challenge of Retaining Customers Acquired with Free Trials
finding: Household panel data from a digital television service, modelled with corrections for selection: per authors, customer lifetime value of free-trial customers was on average 59% lower than that of regular customers, but free-trial customers were more responsive to marketing communication and to their own usage rates.
why_for_us: Viewers pulled in by a hook and a free trial are fragile customers; follow-up communication and getting them to actually use the product matter more for them than for others.

title: Try It, You’ll Like It—Or Will You? The Perils of Early Free-Trial Promotions for High-Tech Service Adoption
finding: Structural model and simulations on trial, adoption and usage data for an interactive digital TV service: per authors, free trials are a double-edged sword because a disappointing trial experience can lose a prospect for good, and timing and usage intensity during the trial are key to effectiveness.
why_for_us: Do not drive notaries to a first contact with the product before that first contact is good; a strong opening that leads to a weak first session destroys the lead.

title: Rapid Prediction of Player Retention in Free-to-Play Mobile Games
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment
finding: Per authors, simple heuristic rules using information from the first session, first day and first week of player activity predict short-term retention with performance comparable to common classification algorithms (figures not in the abstract; games, not business software).
why_for_us: First-session behaviour already tells who stays; instrument the first session after the episode's call to action and judge episodes by it, not only by views.

title: Evaluating the Onboarding Phase of Free-toPlay Mobile Games: A Mixed-Method Approach
venue: Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play
finding: Lab-based mixed-methods study of onboarding: the part of the abstract read states that the first few minutes of play typically show substantial churn among new players and presents an approach to evaluate that phase; no effect sizes were available (games context, small-scale lab work).
why_for_us: Only indirect support for 'the first minutes decide'; use as a pointer to onboarding evaluation methods, not as proof for SaaS.

title: Personalization in Email Marketing: The Role of Noninformative Advertising Content
finding: Randomised field experiments with three companies and millions of recipients: per authors, adding the recipient's name to the subject line raised opens by 20% (9.05% to 10.80%), sales leads by 31% (0.39% to 0.51%) and cut unsubscribes by 17% (1.2% to 1.0%).
why_for_us: Putting the notary's name in the subject line was worth about +1.75 percentage points of opens in this setting; cheap to do, but see OU047 for a failed reproduction.

title: Personalized subject lines in email marketing
finding: Field replication of Sahni et al. (2018): per authors, there was no indication that the recipient's first name in the subject line improved open or click-through rates, whereas using the surname had a positive effect on both (sample size not in the abstract).
why_for_us: First-name personalisation may have worn out; for notaries a formal surname/title form ('Pani Notariusz Kowalska'-style address) is the variant worth testing.

title: Should I open this email? inbox-level cues, curiosity and attention to email
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Think-aloud study plus experiment manipulating message importance, subject-line specificity, workload and personal utility: per authors, uncertainty about content at inbox level increased the likelihood of attention to a message, but this effect diminished with stronger task and personal utility cues and higher demand (sample size not in the abstract).
why_for_us: A vague, curiosity-style subject helps only when the recipient is not busy and no utility cue is present; busy professionals respond to stated usefulness, so lead the subject with the concrete benefit.

title: May I have your attention, please? An investigation on opening effectiveness in e-mail marketing
finding: Observational OLS analysis of 5,765 promotional e-mails sent 2013-2018 by multinational companies to 455 million users in 73 countries: per authors, mailing frequency and use of segmentation significantly affect open rates, and every e-mail sent carries a hidden opportunity cost (correlational, not experimental).
why_for_us: Open rates depend on how often we mail and how well the list is segmented at least as much as on wording; send episode announcements sparingly and to a notary-only segment.

title: Dismissed! a detailed exploration of how mobile phone users handle push notifications
venue: International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction with Mobile Devices and Services (MobileHCI)
finding: Field log study (794,525 notifications, 278 users): per authors, users received a median of 56 notifications per day, messaging apps generated most of them, and other notification types rarely led to a conversion (rates between about 15 and 25%).
why_for_us: A push or app notification about a new episode competes with dozens of others and most non-message notifications are not acted on; do not rely on notifications as the main entry to an episode.

title: The skipping behavior of users of music streaming services and its relation to musical structure
finding: Streaming-service behavioural data (authors affiliated with Spotify; sample size not in the abstract): per authors, the distribution over time of skip events correlates with the musical structure of a song, is specific to each song, and is independent of user cohort and date of observation.
why_for_us: Drop-off points are a property of the content's structure, not of the audience; read each episode's retention curve against its beats and fix the beat where people leave.

title: Drawing listener attention in popular music: Testing five musical features arising from the theory of attention economy
finding: Corpus studies: in 303 U.S. top-10 singles 1986-2015, features such as time before the voice enters and time before the title is mentioned changed in a direction favouring attention grabbing, per the author; but in 60 popular vs 60 less popular 2015 songs by the same artists the data supported none of the hypotheses.
why_for_us: Shorter intros are an industry trend, not a demonstrated cause of success; 'get the voice in immediately' is reasonable practice but unproven as a driver of popularity.

title: Trust in artificial voices: A "congruency effect" of first impressions and behavioural experience
finding: Three iterated investment-game experiments with agents differing in accent or in natural vs synthetic voice (short conference paper): per authors, participants trusted the agent with one voice more when it behaved trustworthily and the agent with the other voice more when it behaved untrustworthily, i.e. trust depended on congruency between behaviour and the voice's first impression.
why_for_us: The AI voice sets an expectation that later content is checked against; a very trustworthy-sounding voice followed by a let-down is punished, so match the voice to what the character and the product actually do.

title: The impact of the sonic logo’s acoustic features on orienting responses, emotions and brand personality transmission
finding: Within-subject lab experiment with 18 voiceless sonic-logo versions (electrodermal activity, heart rate, self-report): per authors, fast-paced logos increased electrodermal activity, slow-paced long logos decreased heart rate, fade-up pitch-ascending fast logos were rated more exciting and descending-pitch ones more pleasant; authors warn of possible participant fatigue.
why_for_us: For the series' opening sound: a short, fast, fade-up ascending sting to orient attention while the series is new; a slower one only once it is recognised.

title: The recall and recognition of sonic logos.
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics Creativity and the Arts
finding: Online experiments (N = 1,860, 90 commercial sonic logos, continuous recognition and sung recall tasks): per authors, recognisability and recallability vary reliably across logos; greater melodic structural complexity enhanced recognition but hindered sung recall.
why_for_us: Decide what the series jingle is for: a slightly more complex motif is better recognised when heard again, a simple one is easier to hum; for a recurring opening sound recognition is the relevant goal.
